extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (PIs) considering whether to resubmit or submit a new application, especially R01 applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for deciding whether to revise/resubmit an NIH grant (A1) or write a new submission (A0), taking into account percentiles, paylines, study section fit, revision effort, timing, and investigator status. Focused on R01-style competing applications in the NIH review system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available revision cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: I think you still have to use your available revision cycles. It is crazy not to because that is the only way to guarantee it will not be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default strategy should be to resubmit when feasible — not resubmitting guarantees zero chance of funding. Consider individual circumstances, but generally use the allowed amendment (A1) opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time required to revise versus write new
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a month between the new-submission receipt date and the revised-application receipt date. You really should be able to revise a grant in a month so I'm not seeing the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic calculation: revising typically takes less time than preparing a full new application; if you can accomplish a substantive revision within the month window, resubmission is often preferable to starting a new proposal. Factor in SRO/summary statement delays which may compress available time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile/score threshold for deciding to resubmit
rubrics_metrics.description: The cutoff score for resubmit as an A1 is probably 40. With an initial score of a 40, the resubmission has about a 50% chance of getting funded. Given paylines at the 10-15%, this is a good use of time. Lower than 40, and I think the numbers probably support revising as a new grant application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical funding-outcome data and local payline context to set a rough percentile cutoff (around the 30–40% range suggested by commenters). If your percentile is near that cutoff, resubmitting as an A1 can be efficient; far below, consider writing a new application targeted differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider institute payline differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ICs are using looser paylines for A0s than for A1s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the specific IC payline policies: if the institute favors original (A0) submissions with looser paylines, that affects the calculus of A1 resubmission versus new submission. Local institute differences can make general NIH-wide stats misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section fit and potential retargeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting a grant funded may in some cases have less to do with rewriting and more to do with getting it in front of a different study section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the summary statement suggests the grant was poorly targeted, submitting a new application aimed at a different, more appropriate study section can be preferable to a simple A1 that stays with the same reviewers. Consider whether resubmission will allow better placement; sometimes writing a new application targeted differently is better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of revision needed (minor vs major overhaul)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count me from triaged to funded in one easy step... if you haul ass and make major overhaul, along with significantly more preliminary data, another pub, etc, it's worthwhile to resubmit an application that's been triaged. It's understandable that those numbers in the graph are daunting, but it's not the stats you should worry about, it's your grant writing and the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only thin edits are needed, the chance of funding is lower and CSR may screen thinly-revised resubmissions out; major overhauls with new data/publications can materially improve chances. Assess whether you can produce genuinely new evidence or a substantive rewrite within the revision cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of similarity screening and 'definition of new grant' rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing titles and Aims is not really that difficult. ... You should check out the guidelines recently published by NIH about 'definition of new grant'. It is damn scary. I have heard that CSR will do as aggressive as they can to 'take out' the 'cheaters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware CSR and NIH policies on what constitutes a 'new' application; attempts to circumvent resubmission limits by minor cosmetic changes risk being flagged. Follow NIH guidance on substantial changes if you intend to submit a new application derived from an earlier one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer turnover effects
rubrics_metrics.description: This has very little to do with how much you improved your grant and everything to do with who rotated off the study section in the interval. Specific people rotating off the study section can easily account for a 30% swing or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that reviewer composition changes between cycles can substantially affect scores independently of changes to the application. This is an unpredictable but real factor supporting the option to resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator status and competing renewal advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: I think the triage to funded is much easier if you are an established investigator and if the grant is a competing renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established investigators and competing renewals often have higher chances of turning a poor score into a funded application on resubmission; early investigators may face different dynamics. Factor PI track record and renewal status into the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO/summary statement timing and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH has been working on speeding up the return of summary statements... The process, at least in general, is that reviewers have an interval... Then the SRO has to compile each one, write a resume of discussion, make sure the review language is not egregious... SROs do not upload the scores. They must turn over to the assistants to upload. It is NIH rule, not SROs' choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays in receiving summary statements and variable quality of SRO-written resumes affect how much time you realistically have to prepare a revision. Account for institutional procedures and delays when planning whether you can do a substantive A1 revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of cumulative low paylines / 'holding pattern'
rubrics_metrics.description: Aren't there way more good grants, backed up and circling in a holding pattern, because they haven't been getting funded? It seems like the cumulative effect of sustained low paylines will get worse and worse over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low paylines create backlog and increased competition over time; even previously marginally fundable resubmissions may face stiffer competition. Use longitudinal funding trends cautiously; local study sections or ICs may deviate from NIH-wide patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit tradeoff versus producing papers or preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to think for yourself how the balance of revising a grant, writing up another paper or generating data works out in your own specific circumstances. (Just don't overcredit the value of another paper or more preliminary data, as is my constant refrain.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate opportunity costs: time spent revising vs generating publications or new data. Do not overvalue an extra paper if it doesn't materially change fundability; focus on changes that reviewers will find persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't assume triage equals hopelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: I don't think I've ever had a grant that was initially triaged get funded but of course some of that is bias in what I chose to pursue. I have at least one that went from 51%ile to funded and another that went from 48%ile to a very close miss on the funding line... I am aware of multiple instances of initially triaged grants getting funded on the next submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial triage does not preclude later funding after substantial revision; cases exist where triaged applications later succeeded. Consider possibility of turnaround especially if major improvements are feasible.
